verses.translation_literal: And Abraham added and took a wife, and her name [was] Keturah.
verses.translation_dramatic: The old man was not finished. Sarah was in the earth at Machpelah, Isaac had a wife by the well, and still Abraham rose and took another woman into his tents. Her name was Keturah: Incense.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb 'added' (wayyosef) is the language of someone who does more of what he has already done; the KJV's 'Then again' captures the sense but hides that the narrator sets this beside the earlier chapters of long barrenness: after a lifetime of waiting for one child, Abraham now fathers a household. The KJV says 'wife', and the Hebrew does say 'ishah, wife, but this is the same woman who in v. 6 and in 1 Chronicles 1:32 is a pilegesh, a secondary wife without the inheritance rights of the principal wife. An ancient hearer would hear that status gap in the very next verses. Keturah's name comes from the root q-t-r, 'to smoke', and keturah is the word for incense: a name that sells the scene before she speaks. Rashi, following Genesis Rabbah, identifies her with Hagar; Rashbam, Ibn Ezra and Radak reject that, and the plain text gives a new woman with a new name. Do not play her as a footnote: the six sons that follow will become the caravan peoples of the eastern desert.

philological_notes.note: 'He added': used with a second verb to mean 'he did again'. Here it follows the narrative of Sarah's burial and Isaac's marriage and marks a new chapter in Abraham's household.

From the root 'to smoke, to burn incense'. The name means roughly 'perfumed' or 'incense'. Rashi (after Genesis Rabbah) reads it as a nickname for Hagar, because her deeds were as fragrant as incense; the plain sense is a proper name.

verses.translation_literal: And she bore to him [obj] Zimran and [obj] Jokshan and [obj] Medan and [obj] Midian and [obj] Ishbak and [obj] Shuah.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Keturah bore him sons, one after another: Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah. Six names, spoken like a tally of tents.
verses.directors_commentary: A bare list, but a list is a statement. Six sons dwarf the single sons of Sarah and Hagar, and the narrator gives them names that will turn into places and peoples: Midian and Medan will matter again in Judges, Exodus and Genesis 37, where Midianite traders buy Joseph. The KJV's 'she bare him' is faithful; what it cannot show is the repeated 'et', the object marker, which turns the list into a drumbeat of separate arrivals. Sforno argues the children were raised in Abraham's house though they were not his in the strict sense; that is his reading, set against Chronicles. Play this as a quick, proud recital, not a sentimental scene: the point is Abraham's fruitfulness after the covenant promise of many nations (Gen 17:4).

philological_notes.note: Midian, ancestor of the Midianites. The name is spelled almost like Medan (mdn) just before it; the two names may be variants of one root, 'strife, judgment'.

verses.translation_literal: And Jokshan fathered [obj.] Sheba and [obj.] Dedan; and [the] sons of Dedan were Asshurim and Letushim and Leummim.
verses.translation_dramatic: Jokshan, in his turn, fathered sons: Sheba, and Dedan. And Dedan's sons were Asshurim, and Letushim, and Leummim. The names come three together, plural in their very endings, like a crowd already gathering at the tent door.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a genealogy, and it works by ear. Each name is a stone set in a line, and the line shows how far Abraham's household has spread by the time he dies. Dedan's three sons end in the plural -im, which is unusual for the name of one man. The Hebrew says plainly they 'were' (hayu) these three, and Ramban notes that this verb sets them apart from the usual 'fathered' (compare Genesis 10:13).

The reading is old and divided. Onkelos treats them as common nouns: 'camps', 'tent-dwellers' and 'islanders' (Onkelos on Genesis 25:3), and Pseudo-Jonathan has 'traders, merchants and heads of nations'. Rashi, from Genesis Rabbah, takes them as 'heads of nations' and says he cannot square Onkelos with the Hebrew. Ramban explains how Onkelos got there (from the roots of 'step', 'cast about' and 'island') but then sides with Rashi and Ibn Ezra: they are names and carry no descriptive sense. Radak is puzzled only by the plural form and suggests the usage was known to the family. Play them as people, not as job titles.

The KJV is right to transliterate and not to translate them, and so follows the majority view. Its 'begat' is an archaism for the plain yalad, 'fathered'; and it renders hayu as 'were' without remarking that the verse changes from 'fathered' to 'were', which is the very point that troubled the commentators.

philological_notes.note: A plural-form name, not the Assyrians (Ashur, spelled differently). Onkelos translates it as 'camps', as if from 'ashur, a step, so travellers' stages; Ramban explains this by the roots in Job 23:11 and Psalm 37:31, but the same Ramban holds that the word is a name. Rashi cannot fit Onkelos to the Hebrew and reads 'heads of nations'. Ibn Ezra reports that some read 'guides who know the roads' and says the correct view is that they are names.

Onkelos has 'tent-dwellers' (shekunin); Rashi, too, explains them as tent-owners who scatter hither and thither, from netushim, 'scattered' (1 Samuel 30:16), lamed and nun being interchangeable. The same root can mean 'to sharpen' (1 Samuel 13:20; Job 16:9), which Ramban says some translators used for 'wicked men with burning faces'. Ramban nevertheless takes the word as a name.

verses.translation_literal: And the sons of Midian: Ephah and Epher and Hanoch and Abida and Eldaah. All these [were] sons of Keturah.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the sons of Midian: Ephah, and Epher, and Hanoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All of these, every one, were sons of Keturah.
verses.directors_commentary: The list closes with a ledger's summary: 'all these'. Radak notes that the verse counts sons and grandsons together under her name, sixteen in all, which is why 'sons of Keturah' stretches across generations. The KJV renders 'children of Keturah', which blurs the Hebrew 'sons'. Ephah is one of the peoples who bring camels, gold and incense in Isaiah 60:6, and Midian will later appear in the Joseph story and in Moses' exile. Here the narrator is clearing the ground before turning to Isaac, the heir: Abraham's other lines are named, counted and set aside.

verses.translation_literal: And Abraham gave [obj] all that [was] his to Isaac.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Abraham gave to Isaac everything that was his. All of it. The flocks, the tents, the silver, the promise: everything.
verses.directors_commentary: Short, flat, final. The verb 'gave' (yitten) is the same verb that will govern the next verse, and the contrast is the point: to Isaac, 'all that he had'; to the other sons, 'gifts'. In the ancient world a father could assign his estate in life by a gift, and Radak reads this as avoiding quarrels after death; Sforno in v. 6 says Abraham used the language of gift rather than inheritance so that his arrangements could not be contested. The KJV 'all that he had' is accurate. Play it as a quiet, decisive act, not a drama: the covenant line already passes to Isaac by God's word (Gen 21:12), and this is its legal expression.

verses.translation_literal: And to the sons of the concubines who [belonged] to Abraham, Abraham gave gifts, and he sent them away from upon Isaac his son, while he [was] still alive, eastward, to the land of the east.
verses.translation_dramatic: But to the sons of the concubines, Abraham gave gifts. Gifts, and no more than gifts. And while he still drew breath, while his own eyes could still see it done, he sent them away from Isaac his son. Away from the tents, away from the wells, away from the promise. East they went, toward the rising sun, into the land of the east.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a scene of division carried out by an old man who knows exactly what he is doing. Abraham has just made Isaac heir of everything (25:5); now he deals with the others, and the verb is blunt. Hebrew שלח in the intensive stem (vayshaleChem) is the word for dismissing, releasing, driving off, the same verb used for sending Hagar away in Genesis 21. The KJV's 'sent them away' is accurate but gentle; play it as a dismissal. The reason is ancient inheritance practice. A father with sons by several women could divide his estate while alive, and a gift given in life, unlike a share at death, closed the claim. Abraham does it 'while still alive' so that no one can contest it afterward. Sforno draws the same conclusion: the gifts were not in the language of inheritance at all, so that his arrangement would stand; Radak adds that Isaac was to be spared the burden and any quarrel over the estate. Wealth here is livestock, silver and gold, which is what Radak says the gifts consisted of.

The word 'concubines' needs care. The KJV's 'concubines' is right, but it carries a lurid sense that the Hebrew pilegesh does not: a legitimate secondary wife whose sons do not inherit the main line. Ramban argues that every wife of Abraham counts as a concubine here because only Isaac's line carries the covenant (Genesis 21:12), even Keturah, whom Genesis 25:1 calls a wife. Rashi, following Genesis Rabbah, claims the text is written defective, with a single concubine, Hagar who is Keturah; but Radak, on Genesis 25:1, says he found it written full, with the yod, in all the accurate manuscripts, and our Hebrew text agrees. So the plural stands. The KJV also flattens a sound play: qedmah ('eastward') and 'erets qedem ('the land of the east') share one root, and the Hebrew rings it twice. 'Unto the east country' is fair, but it loses the echo. Qedem is also 'before, ancient': the sons go toward the old country, which Radak identifies with the lands of Abraham's own family, so that they live among kin. Nothing in the verse says they were unwilling; it says only that the distance is the point.

The verse also tells the audience something about time. 'While he is still alive' puts this just before Abraham's death in verses 7 to 8, so the scene belongs to his final years. He is a hundred and seventy-some and still managing the household.

philological_notes.note: 'The concubines': a secondary wife without the inheritance rights of the principal wife. Rashi, on Genesis 25:6, reports the Midrash that the word is written defective and so means one concubine only, Hagar who is Keturah; Radak, on Genesis 25:1, answers that he found it written full, with the yod, in all the accurate manuscripts. Ramban holds that 'concubine' marks a wife whose children are not heirs of the covenant.

Intensive (Piel) form of 'send': to dispatch, dismiss, send off for good, rather than simply to send. The same stem is used in Genesis 21:14 for Hagar. The Piel gives the sense of an act decided and completed.

A directional ה ('eastward') followed by 'to the land of the east', both on the root of 'front, before, ancient'. Radak reads the first phrase as the direction and the second as the region, the country of Abraham's kin (Haran and Ur of the Chaldees).

verses.translation_literal: And these [are] the days of the years of the life of Abraham which he lived: a hundred year and seventy year and five years.
verses.translation_dramatic: And these were the days of Abraham's life, all the years he lived: a hundred years, and seventy years, and five years more.
verses.directors_commentary: The text weighs the life in three heaps, a hundred, seventy and five, so that the number is heard as a long accumulation, not as one figure; the KJV's 'an hundred threescore and fifteen' is the same sum in archaic dress. 'The days of the years of the life' is a formal funerary frame, the way an obituary opens in the Torah. Rashi hears moral weight in the three heaps (age 100 like age 70 and age 70 like age 5, without sin). At 175 Abraham is thirty years short of his father Terah's 205 (Gen 11:32), and by the chronology of the text his twin grandsons Jacob and Esau, born when he was 160, are fifteen. Leave a beat after the number: a life is being closed.

philological_notes.note: 'Years of the life of': a fixed formula that opens the obituary notices of the patriarchs (cf. Gen 23:1, 47:28). The plural 'chayyim' (life) is an intensive plural.

verses.translation_literal: And Abraham expired and died in a good grey-hair, old and satisfied; and he was gathered to his peoples.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Abraham breathed out his last, and died: in a good old age, an old man and full, content with his days. And he was gathered to his people.
verses.directors_commentary: Two verbs, not one: 'expired' (gava') and 'died' (met). Ibn Ezra and Radak say gava' is the quick, painless death, a breath leaving the body, not a long illness; the KJV's 'gave up the ghost' is an English idiom that adds a spirit the verb does not name. 'Good grey-hair' (seivah tovah) was promised to Abraham in Gen 15:15, and the narrator now confirms it. 'Satisfied' (saveya') is the word for being full of food: Ramban reads it as a life that wanted nothing more. The KJV's 'full of years' fills in a noun that the Hebrew leaves out; the Hebrew simply says 'old and satisfied'. 'His peoples' is plural: it names the family dead who have gone before, and it happens before the burial in v. 9, so it cannot mean the grave. Ibn Ezra offers two readings, honour of the soul or simply the idiom for joining his fathers; Sforno reads it as the afterlife. Leave a pause and let the plural land.

philological_notes.note: 'He expired': a verb for breathing one's last, used of the flood dead (Gen 7:21) and of Jacob (Gen 49:33). Ibn Ezra says every gava' is a death but not every death is gava'; it marks a quick, easy end.

'And he was gathered to his peoples': a plural of 'am (kin). The phrase precedes the burial and so describes joining the family dead, not the grave. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Sforno differ on whether it hints at an afterlife.

verses.translation_literal: And they buried him, Isaac and Ishmael his sons, to the cave of Machpelah, to the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, which [is] upon the face of Mamre.
verses.translation_dramatic: And his sons buried him, Isaac and Ishmael, side by side, in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron, son of Zohar the Hittite, the field that faces Mamre.
verses.directors_commentary: The two brothers who were separated by Sarah's anger, and by Hagar's flight into the wilderness, stand at one grave. The narrator names Isaac first and Ishmael second, and calls both 'his sons': the Hebrew puts them under one verb, and Ramban records the midrash that the son of the maidservant gave honour to the son of the mistress. Rashi reads Ishmael's presence as proof that he turned back to God (teshuvah), and leads Isaac before him. The KJV 'before Mamre' obscures a literal face: the field is 'on the face of Mamre', as if it looks at it. The whole address is deliberately legal: the name, the father's name, and the clan are given as they were in the sale contract in chapter 23, so the audience hears property and not only sorrow. Radak notes that 'to the cave, to the field' means 'in the cave in the field'.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'upon the face of Mamre'. The same formula is used in the sale narrative of chapter 23. It places the field facing, east of, Mamre near Hebron.

verses.translation_literal: The field which Abraham acquired from [with] the sons of Heth; there Abraham was buried, and Sarah his wife.
verses.translation_dramatic: The field Abraham had bought from the sons of Heth: there Abraham was laid, and Sarah his wife beside him.
verses.directors_commentary: The narrator repeats the purchase to remind us that this earth is bought, not promised: Abraham, the man to whom God promised the whole land, owned only a field for his grave. Radak says that whenever the Torah mentions the burial here it mentions the purchase, to show Abraham's love of the land and that he did not doubt the promise even while owning only a tomb. 'From with the sons of Heth' (me'et) is a deliberate phrase of a legal purchase made in the gate. The KJV 'purchased' is fine; 'acquired' is closer to qanah, which also means 'to get, to create'. The couple are named together at the end, and the word order puts Sarah last, as the one who was laid there first.

philological_notes.note: A passive (Pual) form: 'was buried'. Radak observes that the singular verb with two subjects follows the nearer one, Abraham, and applies to Sarah too.

verses.translation_literal: And it was after the death of Abraham, and God blessed Isaac his son; and Isaac dwelt with Beer-lahai-roi.
verses.translation_dramatic: And it came to pass, after Abraham was dead, that God blessed Isaac his son. And Isaac settled beside Beer-lahai-roi, the well of the Living One who sees me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The funeral is over, and the first line after it is the blessing. 'God blessed Isaac' is the answer to the question hanging over the whole chapter: Abraham has given Isaac every possession (v. 5) but a blessing is not a possession, and here it comes from God directly. Radak reads 'blessed' as 'made him prosper as he had made his father prosper'.

The rabbis ask why the blessing waited until Abraham was dead. Rashi, from Sotah 14a, says God comforted him as one comforts mourners; and adds a second answer: although God had handed the blessings to Abraham, Abraham was afraid to bless Isaac because he foresaw Esau coming from him, and so said, 'Let the Master of the blessings come and bless whom he pleases.' That is Rashi's reason. Pseudo-Jonathan gives a different one: Abraham was unwilling to bless Ishmael, and if he blessed Isaac and not Ishmael, Ishmael would bear him a grudge, so he blessed neither; and after his death the LORD blessed Isaac. Keep both as readings; the Hebrew states no reason.

The KJV's 'dwelt by the well Lahai-roi' swallows the first word of a name: it is Beer-lahai-roi, the well Hagar named in Genesis 16:14, so Isaac settles at the place where the rejected mother met God. 'Dwelt' is yashav, to sit, to settle, to take up residence. The preposition is 'im, 'with'; Radak says it means 'at', as in 'know with your heart' (Deuteronomy 8:5), and Ramban says Isaac pitched his tent next to the well, since it was not a town. The BBE drops the well altogether. Here the narrator says 'God' (Elohim), not the personal name; Onkelos, by contrast, writes the LORD.

philological_notes.note: 'And he blessed.' The verb is said of God and takes Isaac as its object, marked by the object marker. Radak understands it as practical success, in the way his father succeeded. Rashi (Sotah 14a) hears here the consolation due to a mourner, and Abraham's fear of Esau; Pseudo-Jonathan hears Abraham's unwillingness to bless Ishmael.

'With', used here in the sense of 'at, beside'. Radak compares Deuteronomy 8:5 ('know with your heart') and Genesis 35:4 ('the oak that is with Shechem'), and reads it as the preposition 'in'. Ramban says that since the well is not a town, 'with' means he pitched his tent beside it, near that place.

verses.translation_literal: And these [are] the generations of Ishmael son of Abraham, whom Hagar the Egyptian, maidservant of Sarah, bore to Abraham.
verses.translation_dramatic: And these are the generations of Ishmael, Abraham's son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's maidservant, bore to Abraham.
verses.directors_commentary: A new section opens with the formula 'these are the generations' (toledot), the same heading the book uses to mark each family line: here the line of the son who is sent aside. The verse is a full legal identification, a chain of names and statuses: Ishmael, son of Abraham, son of Hagar, an Egyptian, Sarah's slave-girl. The KJV 'handmaid' is softer than shifchah, a servant woman owned by her mistress. Rashbam notes the difference with Isaac: Ishmael is described by his mother because he is not the line through which the covenant runs, while Isaac is defined by his father. Radak says the Torah honours Ishmael as Abraham's firstborn and as the father of the twelve princes God had promised (Gen 17:20). Hagar's foreignness and her slavery are stated plainly, as the text insists on the whole picture, with no apology.

philological_notes.note: 'Generations, accounts': the structural heading of Genesis, from the root 'to bear'. It introduces what came out of a person, his descendants and their story.
A female servant owned by a household, distinct from 'amah. The KJV 'handmaid' softens the sense of ownership.

verses.translation_literal: And these [are] the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, by their begettings: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam,
verses.translation_dramatic: And these are the names of the sons of Ishmael, each in his own name, each in the order of his birth. First came Nebaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael; then Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a roll call, and it should be played as one: a father's line unrolled name by name, with a small pause on the first. The text turns Ishmael's household into a register the way an ancient clan archive would, and the order matters. Rashi and Radak both read 'by their begettings' as birth order, with Nebaioth the firstborn.

The KJV is accurate here but flattens a repetition. The Hebrew says 'names' twice in a row ('the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names'), a formula of completeness rather than padding, and it uses 'toledot' (begettings, generations) as the structural word that will cut the whole book into sections. The unusual feature is that Ishmael, the excluded son, receives a full 'toledot' list at all. Genealogy in this world is title to existence: a name on the list means a people.

philological_notes.note: 'According to their begettings', that is, in birth order. Rashi on Genesis 25:13 reads it as the order of their birth, one after another; Radak on Genesis 25:13 agrees and adds that the firstborn was Nebaioth.

verses.translation_literal: And Mishma, and Dumah, and Massa,
verses.translation_dramatic: And Mishma, and Dumah, and Massa,
verses.directors_commentary: Keep the list moving; the verse is three names and no verb, and the actor should let the 'and' do the walking. There is nothing here for the KJV to soften. The only thing worth hearing is the sound: Dumah (which resembles the Hebrew word for 'silence') and Massa (which is also the word for 'burden' or 'oracle') are names that later biblical writers can play on. In the text itself they are simply sons.

verses.translation_literal: Hadad, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hadad, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
verses.directors_commentary: The list lets go of its 'and' for two names, Jetur and Naphish, and then returns to it for the last: a rhythm of a list nearing its end, with Kedemah closing it. The sound of 'Kedemah' is 'eastward', so the list ends facing the east where these sons will live. The KJV, YLT and Webster read 'Hadar' where the Hebrew in front of us reads Hadad; a similar name appears in 1 Chronicles 1:30 as Hadad, and the two letters ד and ר are easily confused in copying. Tema is a name that will later belong to an Arabian oasis, and Jetur and Naphish appear in a later war against the Hagrites (so Radak on Genesis 25:16 points to 1 Chronicles 5:19): these were tribes before they were tour stops.

philological_notes.note: Hadad, not Hadar as in the KJV. The name is that of a well-known West Semitic storm god, so it is a plausible name for an Ishmaelite; the ד/ר confusion behind 'Hadar' is a copyist's error that the KJV inherited. This identification with the storm god is my own reading.

verses.translation_literal: These [are] the sons of Ishmael, and these [are] their names, by their villages and by their encampments: twelve chieftains for their peoples.
verses.translation_dramatic: These, then, were the sons of Ishmael, and these their names, village by village, camp by camp: twelve chieftains, each one at the head of his own people.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a ledger, and it should be played as a fulfilled promise. The word for 'chieftains', nasi'im, is exactly the word God used in Gen 17:20: 'twelve nasi'im shall he father, and I will make him a great nation.' Abraham was told it about Ishmael, and here, as Ishmael's life closes, the count comes out at twelve. The tribal number is a family habit of this book: Nahor's line also reaches twelve sons (Gen 22:20-24, eight by Milcah and four by Reumah), and Jacob's twelve are about to be born in the very next scene. Ishmael's twelve are the blessing kept, listed briefly before the story turns to the son through whom the covenant runs.

The KJV's 'castles' is the main distortion. Tirah is not a fortress: it is a camp or enclosure, and Hebrew sets it beside hatzerim, unwalled villages (Rashi: towns without a wall; Radak: hatzerim are open settlements, tirot the fortified ones). Play it as people who live between tent and village, on the desert edge, with herds and wells, not as barons in keeps. The KJV's 'princes' also overshoots: a nasi' is literally one 'lifted up', a tribal head chosen to carry the group, and 'nations' for le'ummot hides that this is a different word from goyim, a plain 'peoples' or 'clans'. Radak adds that the names mattered for later hearers: wherever a people bore one of these names, they could be known as Ishmael's.

philological_notes.note: From nasa', 'to lift, carry': the one lifted up, the chieftain who bears his clan. The same word promised for Ishmael in Gen 17:20. Radak takes each as head of a large family that bore his name.

An encampment or enclosure, not a castle (KJV). Rashi and Radak pair it with hatzerim (open villages) as the fortified or walled counterpart; Ibn Ezra reads 'palaces'. Here it sits with the village as a settled-or-camped way of life.

verses.translation_literal: And these [are] the years of the life of Ishmael: a hundred year and thirty year and seven years; and he expired, and he died, and he was gathered to his kinspeople.
verses.translation_dramatic: And these were the years of Ishmael's life: a hundred and thirty and seven. Then his breath failed, and he died, and he was gathered to his people.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone drops here: a life added up and closed. Notice the three-step ending, 'expired... died... was gathered', which the text uses for Abraham (25:8) and, later, for Isaac and Jacob. The same funeral formula is given to the outcast son as to the chosen father. That is the statement. The KJV's 'gave up the ghost' is a perfectly good old idiom, but it obscures that the Hebrew has a plain verb 'gava', 'to breathe one's last', followed by 'to die' as its own act.

The tradition argues over why Ishmael's years are counted at all. Rashi (citing the Talmud in the name of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba) uses them to date Jacob's departure; Rashbam says it honours Abraham; Ramban says Scripture records the years of the children of the righteous to show that the seed of the righteous is blessed. Hearing 'gathered to his kinspeople' as the Hebrew does is to hear a plural: 'amav is his peoples, the clan beyond the grave.

philological_notes.note: 'And he expired': to breathe one's last. Rashi on Genesis 25:17 says gevi'ah is said only of the righteous; Ramban on Genesis 25:17 records the Talmudic objection from the flood generation and reads it as a death without long suffering.
'Was gathered to his kinspeople': a passive, with a plural noun, naming burial with the ancestors rather than the grave itself.

verses.translation_literal: And they dwelt from Havilah to Shur, which [is] on the face of Egypt, as you go toward Asshur; on the face of all his brothers he fell.
verses.translation_dramatic: They pitched their tents from Havilah as far as Shur, that wilderness that looks toward Egypt on the road to Asshur. And in the very face of all his brothers, he settled.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the geography of a people who live on edges. Havilah to Shur is a wide band of desert from the Arabian side to the Egyptian frontier, the stretch where Hagar had once fled (Genesis 16:7). 'As you go toward Asshur' is spoken to a traveller: the verse puts the reader on a caravan route.

The last clause is the hard one. 'Al-penei kol-echav nafal' is literally 'on the face of all his brothers he fell'. The KJV and Webster take it as 'he died in the presence of all his brethren', which makes the verse repeat v. 17; the ASV 'abode' and BBE 'took their place' follow Rashi and Radak, who read 'nafal' as 'dwelt', as in Judges 7:12, and who connect it to the angel's words to Hagar, 'he will dwell over against all his brothers' (Genesis 16:12). The change of verb is the point: Rashi says while Abraham lived, Ishmael 'would dwell'; once Abraham died, he 'fell' into his lot. Ibn Ezra offers a third reading, 'fell' as the lot that fell to him. The word carries both the falling of a lot and the falling of a tent-pitcher. Say it as the end of the story of Ishmael: in the face of, against, east of, his brothers, and not at peace with them.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'fell'. Rashi and Radak read it as 'dwelt', comparing Judges 7:12 and the Hagar prophecy of Genesis 16:12; Ibn Ezra allows 'his lot fell' or 'he died'. The KJV 'he died' chooses the plain meaning of the verb but repeats v. 17.

'On the face of', which can mean east of, facing, or in defiance of; the same phrase in Genesis 16:12 is the pivot of the angel's prophecy. The ambiguity between 'opposite' and 'against' is part of the point.

verses.translation_literal: And these [are] the begettings of Isaac, son of Abraham: Abraham fathered Isaac.
verses.translation_dramatic: Now this is the story of Isaac, Abraham's son. Abraham fathered Isaac.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new section begins, and the staging changes: the long caravan-road panorama of Ishmael gives way to a single house. 'Toledot' is the book's section marker, and it means more than 'generations': it is what comes out of someone. The 'generations of Isaac' are therefore mostly the story of his sons, as Rashi and Ramban say (Jacob and Esau).

Then the line that seems redundant: we have just been told Isaac is Abraham's son, and now Abraham fathered Isaac. The tradition fills this in. Rashi, citing the old tale, says scoffers claimed Sarah had conceived by Abimelech and God shaped Isaac's face to resemble Abraham's so all would say 'Abraham fathered Isaac'; Radak adds the sense that he walked in his father's ways. Rashbam gives the plain reading, that unlike Ishmael, who is the son of the Egyptian handmaid, Isaac is the true heir by Abraham's real wife. Ramban notes that this is how Scripture returns to the head of a line when a branch is closed, as in Chronicles. The KJV's 'begat' is archaic but exact.

philological_notes.note: 'Begettings, what comes of someone'; the formula that structures Genesis. Rashi and Ramban on Genesis 25:19 take 'the generations of Isaac' to mean Jacob and Esau.
'Fathered' (hif'il). Ibn Ezra, as quoted by Ramban, allows 'raised, made great', comparing Genesis 50:23; Rashi gives the tale of the resemblance to Abraham.

verses.translation_literal: And Isaac was a son of forty years when he took Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Aramean, from Paddan-aram, sister of Laban the Aramean, to himself for a wife.
verses.translation_dramatic: Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah as his wife: Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram, sister of Laban the Aramean.
verses.directors_commentary:
A marriage told in one breath, with the age given as a stage direction: forty, a man, no longer the boy of Moriah. The verse is overloaded with her pedigree. 'Aramean' appears twice, 'daughter of', 'sister of', 'from Paddan-aram': Rebekah is introduced entirely by the men around her. Rashi asks why this was said again, since the reader already knows, and answers that it is to praise her: the daughter of a wicked man, the sister of a wicked man, in a wicked place, who did not learn from their deeds. Ibn Ezra says Laban was better known than their father.

The KJV's 'Syrian' for 'Aramean' is an anachronism of the Greek and Latin habit of calling Arameans Syrians; the Hebrew says Aramean, the people of the northern Mesopotamian steppe. 'Paddan-aram' is a Genesis name, and Radak ties it to Hosea 12:13, where Jacob flees to 'the field of Aram'; Rashi and Radak offer 'yoke of oxen', 'field', or two Arams paired, and the point is the region around Haran. Forty also begins the clock on the barrenness: Rashbam adds this age to Isaac's age at the twins' birth (sixty) and gets twenty childless years.

philological_notes.note: Rashi on Genesis 25:20 gives 'pair of oxen' (two Arams, Naharaim and Zobah) or 'field of Aram'; Radak on Genesis 25:20 cites Hosea 12:13 for the field reading. Region around Haran. The exact etymology is unsettled.
'The Aramean'; the KJV 'Syrian' translates the same word, an old naming habit rather than a different Hebrew word.

verses.translation_literal: And Isaac pleaded with YHWH opposite his wife, for she [was] barren; and YHWH let himself be pleaded with by him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Isaac pleaded with the LORD, standing before his wife, for she was barren. And the LORD let himself be moved by his plea, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
verses.directors_commentary:
Twenty years of silence end in a single sentence, and it is built on a sound. The verb 'ya'tar' is used twice: 'Isaac pleaded' and 'YHWH was pleaded with', the same root once active and once passive. The prayer and the answer are one word, turned inside out. The KJV 'intreated' and 'was intreated of him' keeps this, and is the best English for it. Rashi reads the root as pressing, multiplying, to pile up pleas; the sense is a man who wouldn't stop.

Then 'lenokhach ishto'. The KJV 'for his wife' is a guess; the Hebrew says 'opposite' his wife. Rashi pictures the couple standing in two corners praying; Radak gives both 'on her behalf' and that he stood facing her. The scene is a husband and wife at the same altar, not a man who has simply stepped aside. 'Lo', 'to him', also matters: Rashi says the answer came to him and not to her, because the prayer of a righteous man, son of a righteous man, differs from that of a righteous woman, daughter of a wicked one. The barrenness is the setting of the whole patriarchal cycle: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel. Each time the heir comes only because God intervenes.

philological_notes.note: 'Pleaded, entreated'; the verb recurs as a passive in the same verse, 'was entreated'. Rashi on Genesis 25:21 takes the root as multiplication and pressing in prayer; Ibn Ezra takes the second as a nif'al, 'was appeased'.
'Opposite his wife': Rashi on Genesis 25:21 sees them praying in separate corners; Radak on Genesis 25:21 gives 'on her behalf' or 'facing her'.
'Barren', literally rooted-out or uprooted; the standing condition of the matriarchs.

token_glosses.gloss: and [he] let himself be pleaded with

verses.translation_literal: And the sons crushed one another within her, and she said, If so, why [is] this I? And she went to seek YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the children thrashed inside her, driving against one another. And she cried out, "If it is so, why am I?" And she went to seek the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the text breaks off in the middle of a sentence, and a good actor will let it. 'Im-ken lamah zeh anokhi', literally 'if so, why this, I?', has no object and no verb: it is a cry. Rebekah has just got what she prayed for, and it hurts. The KJV 'why am I thus?' makes it a complaint about a sensation; the ASV 'wherefore do I live?' turns it into a cry against life. The tradition splits: Rashi hears a woman asking why she prayed for pregnancy; Ibn Ezra, via the other women she asked; Ramban rejects both and takes it as 'why am I at all?', borrowing Job 10:19. The Hebrew can carry all of these, and the staging should not choose.

'Vayitrotzatzu' is also a sound: a reflexive of 'ratzatz', crush, shatter, with the repeated tz; Rashbam and Ibn Ezra hear instead 'run' (ratz), as if they ran at one another inside her. Both stay in the ear. The 'sons' are called sons before they are born, as Ibn Ezra notes, 'by their end'. And 'to seek YHWH' ('lidrosh') is a trip to an oracle: Rashi sends her to the house of study of Shem, Rashbam to the prophets of those days, and Ramban says the verb means only prayer.

philological_notes.note: 'Crushed one another', reflexive of 'ratzatz'. Rashbam and Ibn Ezra hear a play with 'ratz', to run, as in two runners meeting in a womb; Radak says they seemed to run toward each other.
A broken, elliptical cry. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Ramban give three different readings (longing for pregnancy; asking other women; 'why do I exist'), and the five English versions split likewise.
'To seek, consult'; Ramban on Genesis 25:22 finds the verb used for YHWH only in the sense of prayer, Rashbam of going to the prophets.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH said to her: Two nations [are] in your womb, and two peoples from your inward parts will be separated; and people than people will be stronger, and the great [one] will serve the young [one].
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD said to her: "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples, from within you, will be parted. One people will be stronger than the other, and the elder will serve the younger."
verses.directors_commentary:
The first thing God says in this chapter is the whole plot, in poetry. It comes in four short lines, and it is the only place in the story where the ancient oracle form is heard: parallel lines, doubled terms, a riddle in the last line. Treat it as a spoken oracle, not a conversation. Notice who is addressed: the mother, not the father who prayed.

The KJV 'two manner of people' is a Jacobean flourish for 'two peoples', and its 'the elder shall serve the younger' commits to a reading the Hebrew does not. 'Rav ya'avod tza'ir' is, word for word, 'great will serve small', with no object marker, so grammar alone does not say who serves whom. Radak admits this openly, and argues that the order of the words (subject first) points to the elder serving the younger, but that the prophecy is unclear on purpose because the roles reverse in David's day. The audience, who knows the story, hears the reversal of the ancient rule of the firstborn. 'Le'om mile'om ye'ematz' is also a sound-chain: leom, mile'om, ye'ematz.

The written text has 'gei'im' (proud ones) and the Qere is 'goyim' (nations). Radak records the rabbinic reading of the written form as proud ones, but the Qere stands. 'Goy' is a political nation; 'le'om' (Rashi: kingdom, rule) a people; the doubling is style, says Radak. A third point for the audience: the word 'separated' means the womb is where two peoples begin to divide, which Radak and Ramban read as the sign of the struggle just felt.

philological_notes.note: Read 'nations'; the written consonants have two yods, which Rashi and Radak on Genesis 25:23 take as 'proud ones' (gei'im), a midrash on Rabbi and Antoninus. The reading adopted here is the Qere.

'The great will serve the small': the verse has no object marker, so who serves whom is open grammatically. Radak on Genesis 25:23 says it is unclear and that the order of words points to the elder serving the younger.
'Will be separated': Rashi on Genesis 25:23 reads that they part already in the womb, one to wickedness and one to integrity; Radak sees it as they emerge different, one red and hairy.

verses.translation_literal: And her days to give birth were filled, and behold: twins in her womb.
verses.translation_dramatic: And when her days were full and the hour of birth had come, behold: twins, there in her womb.
verses.directors_commentary:
The word 'hinneh', behold, is the actor's cue. For nine months the oracle has been in the air, and now the midwives see it with their eyes. Rashbam says 'behold' is the usual note of surprise at a discovery, as when Jacob wakes beside Leah. Everyone has been told, and they are still startled.

The KJV 'when her days to be delivered were fulfilled' is fine. What it cannot show is a spelling. The Hebrew writes 'tomim' without the alef, a short form of 'teomim' (twins). Rashi and Radak build a midrash on the missing letter: only one of the pair is righteous, whereas Tamar's twins in Genesis 38:27 are spelled in full because both were. Ibn Ezra treats it simply as the dropping of a root letter. The reader should hear the oracle of the previous verse close on the womb, with the birth itself deferred to the next verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Twins', written without the alef of the root. Rashi and Radak on Genesis 25:24 draw a midrash from the defective spelling, contrasting Tamar's full spelling in Genesis 38:27; Ibn Ezra treats it as an elided root letter.

verses.translation_literal: And the first came out ruddy, all of him like a cloak of hair; and they called his name Esau.
verses.translation_dramatic: The first came out red, red from head to foot, and wrapped in hair as thick as a cloak. Then they named him Esau.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two details make this baby strange, and the actors should find both. He is 'ruddy' (admoni), and he is covered, 'all of him', in hair, as if born already dressed. The Hebrew word for what he wears is adderet, a mantle or cloak, a garment with presence. It is the word used elsewhere for a prophet's hairy cloak and for a fine imported robe (Zech 13:4; Josh 7:21), and, later, for Elijah's mantle, so the audience hears a body that looks like clothing. The KJV's 'an hairy garment' is accurate in sense but flattens the image to a coat; 'red' also loses the diminutive-sounding -oni ending (Ibn Ezra), a ruddiness that clings to him.

Then comes the naming, and the Hebrew gives no explanation, unlike Jacob (v. 26) and 'Edom' (v. 30). The plural 'they called' leaves the namers open: Rashi says everyone who saw him, Radak the onlookers, or Isaac and Rebekah. Rashi hears 'asui, 'made, finished', a child born fully formed with a man's hair. A hearer will also catch the colour and the hair echoing later names: adom/Edom, red, and se'ar/Seir, hairy, the hill country where he will live. Hold that as the audience's ear, not the narrator's statement. Rashi's reading of the red as a sign of bloodshed is a rabbinic foreshadowing, not in the verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Ruddy', from adom, red. The -oni ending is an adjectival formation (Ibn Ezra compares akhzari, cruel). Radak: most newborns are reddish, so the word says strongly red. It plants the root of Edom (v. 30).
'Like a cloak of hair': adderet is a mantle, here of fleece-like hair. Radak pictures it hung with curls of wool. Se'ar, 'hair', sounds like Seir, the land linked to Esau later.
The text gives no etymology here. Rashi and Rashbam hear 'asui, 'made, complete', a baby born already like a grown man with his hair.

verses.translation_literal: And after that his brother came out, and his hand holding on the heel of Esau; and he called his name Jacob; and Isaac [was] a son of sixty years in the bearing of them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And after him, close behind, came his brother, and his small hand was clamped on the heel of Esau, as if he would hold the first-born back, or hold on to him. And so he was named: Jacob, the Heel-Grasper. Isaac was sixty years old on the day they were born to him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image is one of the best stage directions in Genesis: the second twin is born with his fist closed around the first one's heel. The name Ya'aqov is built from 'aqev, 'heel', and Hebrew speakers would also hear the verb 'aqav, 'to follow at the heel, to trip, to cheat'. Esau will say as much in Gen 27:36 ('is he not rightly named Jacob? He has tripped me up these two times'), and Hosea 12:4 turns the birth into an accusation. Rashi and Radak read the grip as an omen: the younger will take what the elder holds. The KJV 'took hold on' is accurate, but its 'his name was called' drops the active 'he called', which leaves open who is naming; Ibn Ezra and Radak say Isaac, Rashi offers God.

The last clause is a piece of bookkeeping that carries drama: Isaac is sixty. Since Abraham was a hundred when Isaac was born (Gen 21:5), Abraham is a hundred and sixty now, and Rebekah has waited twenty years since the marriage (Gen 25:20, 'Isaac was forty'). Radak notes exactly that: twenty years she did not bear. The KJV 'threescore years old' is the right figure in an archaic mould.

philological_notes.note: From 'aqev, 'heel'; the verb 'aqav 'to supplant, to cheat' is the sound the story plays on in Gen 27:36 and Hos 12:4. Sforno ties the name to being 'at the heel, at the end'.
A participle, 'was holding': the hand was still gripping as the child came out, not merely touching.

verses.translation_literal: And the lads grew; and Esau was a man knowing hunting, a man of the field; and Jacob [was] a whole man, dwelling [in] tents.
verses.translation_dramatic: The boys grew, and as they grew they pulled apart. Esau became a man who knew the hunt, a man of the open country, at home where the wind and the wild things were. Jacob was a quiet man, whole and unhurried, who lived among the tents.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two sons are drawn as two ways of life, one of the open country, one of the camp. 'Knowing hunting' (yode'a tsayid) is the language of craft: Esau has the trade. 'Man of the field' (sadeh) is the open land outside settlement, the wild; the KJV's 'cunning hunter' leans on Ibn Ezra's and the Midrash's suspicion of trickery that this verb does not itself carry. Hunting is a trade of ambush, which is why Ibn Ezra hears deceit in it, but the Hebrew only says 'knowing'.

The contrast with Jacob is the point, and here the KJV's 'plain man' is the weakest rendering. Tam is 'complete, whole, without blemish', the word used of Job in Job 1:1 ('blameless'). It does not mean 'plain'. Rashi takes it to mean one not clever at deceit; the Targums go further and make him a student. 'Dwelling tents' is plural: a herdsman moving between tents (Rashbam, Ibn Ezra, comparing 'dweller of tent and cattle', Gen 4:20). The classical readings that put him in a study house are later projection, but the contrast outside/inside is real. Note too that the boys are now na'arim, 'lads'; Rashi dates their parting of ways to age thirteen, and the arithmetic of v.26 puts Abraham's death when they were fifteen.

philological_notes.note: 'Complete, whole, blameless', not 'plain'. Used of Job in Job 1:1. The contrast with Esau is between wholeness and craft, not between boredom and adventure.
'Knowing game / hunting': the participle describes a skill, not a character. Rashi and Ibn Ezra hear trickery in it; the Hebrew does not say so.

verses.translation_literal: And Isaac loved Esau, for game [was] in his mouth; and Rebekah [was] loving Jacob.
verses.translation_dramatic: Isaac loved Esau, for the taste of the hunt was always in his mouth. And Rebekah loved Jacob.
verses.directors_commentary:
The household splits into two pairs, and the Hebrew makes the asymmetry plain: Isaac's love comes with a reason (ki, 'for', 'because'), and Rebekah's with none. The narrator does not give her motive. The KJV makes the cause explicit with a verb the Hebrew does not have ('he did eat of his venison'); the Hebrew idiom is bare: 'game in his mouth'. Whose mouth is disputed. Onkelos, Rashbam, Ibn Ezra and Radak say Isaac's: Esau fed him. Rashi, following the Midrash, says Esau's, because with his mouth he deceived his father, and Pseudo-Jonathan reads it that way (words of trickery in his mouth). Ramban takes it as a figure for constant supply.

An actor needs this: Isaac, old and sedentary (Radak), loves the son who brings him food, and the verbs differ in form, with the narrator writing Isaac's love in the narrative past, 'and he loved', and Rebekah's as a continuing state, 'was loving', a participle. The pair of loves sets up Gen 27 entirely. The nuance that Isaac's affection is tied to appetite, and that Rebekah's is tied to the oracle (Gen 25:23), is Rashbam's.

philological_notes.note: 'Game in his mouth': an idiom; Ramban collects the readings (Isaac's mouth, Esau's mouth, a figure for constancy) and prefers the figure.
A participle: 'was loving', a settled disposition, in contrast to Isaac's narrative 'he loved'.

verses.translation_literal: And Jacob had cooked a stew; and Esau came from the field, and he [was] exhausted.
verses.translation_dramatic: One day Jacob was simmering a stew over the fire. And Esau came in from the open country, and he was spent, drained to the bone.
verses.directors_commentary:
A stage setting in two strokes: smoke and a pot inside, an exhausted man arriving from outside. The verb vayyazed and the noun nazid are the same root: Jacob 'stewed a stew', a cognate pair the KJV renders with the archaic 'sod pottage' ('sod' is the past of 'seethe'). 'Pottage' is also what the Hebrew does not say: nazid is simply a cooked dish. The Hebrew sets Jacob's stillness against Esau's arrival with the abrupt 'and he', a pronoun placed to stress the contrast: and HE, he was exhausted.

'Ayef is bodily exhaustion, not necessarily hunger; Ibn Ezra reads hunger and thirst. Rashi, following the Midrash, makes him 'weary with murder', a reading from Jer 4:31 that the plain narrative does not require, and Pseudo-Jonathan sets the whole scene on the day Abraham died, which would make the stew a mourner's meal. Those are traditions that give the scene a moral frame; the text itself just has a cook, a hunter and a pot. Radak notes the irony of both brothers' characters: Jacob cooks lentils for himself, the plainest food, while Esau is the one driven by appetite.

philological_notes.note: A verb and noun of one root: 'he simmered a simmering'. Radak explains the verb as a variant of 'to boil'; the noun means cooked food, a stew.
'Exhausted, weary'. Ibn Ezra reads thirst and hunger together; Rashi, via the Midrash, reads it as the weariness of violence. The plain sense is simply spent from the field.

verses.translation_literal: And Esau said to Jacob, "Let me swallow, please, some of the red, the red, this, for I [am] weary." Upon thus one called his name Edom.
verses.translation_dramatic: Esau lifted his head and said to Jacob, and the words came cracked and hurried: "Let me gulp it down, please. That red, the red, that there. I am weary." And that is why they called him Edom, the Red One.
verses.directors_commentary:
Esau does not say 'stew', 'soup' or 'lentils'. He says only 'the red, the red, this', pointing and stammering like a man too empty to find the noun. The doubling is the whole performance: play him half-collapsed, grabbing at the colour of the thing instead of its name. The KJV smooths this out. 'Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage' supplies a noun, 'pottage', that Esau never speaks, and 'that same red' flattens the stutter into one tidy phrase. The redness is still there in the KJV, but the broken speech is gone. Only Young's 'this red red thing' keeps the stutter.

The verb is also stronger than 'feed'. Hif'il of la'at, it is found only here, and the rabbis (Rashi, Radak) tie it to the way camels are force-fed (hal'itu), something done to an animal by pouring, not to a guest at a table. Esau asks to be stuffed, and in the same breath he calls himself 'weary' (ayef), the word of exhaustion, a little less than the KJV's 'faint'. The closing line ties his body to his legacy: 'Edom' is the same adom, 'red', that he has just stammered twice, and it sounds like adam and dam, 'man' and 'blood', which the original audience, a people living beside Edom's red sandstone hills, would have heard at once. Rashbam and Ramban hear a taunt in the name, since he traded something great for something small.

philological_notes.note: Hif'il imperative of la'at, 'to swallow, to cram'; it appears only here in the Bible. It is the verb of pouring food into a mouth, not the verb of a polite request. The rabbinic texts cited by Rashi and Radak use it for force-feeding animals.

'The red, the red, this': the adjective is doubled and left without a noun. Rashbam reads the doubling as the speech of a man hurrying to ask; Radak, as the sign of his craving. Whatever the motive, the repeated 'red' is what leads to the name Edom in the same verse.
The name is built on adom 'red', the root of the doubled word above. Jacob's own birth description already had Esau 'red' (admoni, Gen 25:25); the narrator now fixes the name to the stew scene.

verses.translation_literal: And Jacob said, "Sell, as the day, your birthright to me."
verses.translation_dramatic: And Jacob answered, quiet and level: "Sell me your birthright. Sell it to me right now."
verses.directors_commentary:
Jacob's answer is as clipped as Esau's was stammered: one command, one demand, no greeting and no mention of the stew. The word order puts 'to me' last, so the sentence ends on Jacob himself. Play it low and even, the voice of a man who has been waiting for exactly this moment.

The KJV's 'this day' and the ASV's 'first' show how uncertain readers have been about kayyom, literally 'as the day'. Rashi and Radak take it as 'clearly, completely' (a binding sale), Ramban's plain reading is 'at this very time', and the KJV's 'this day' is close to that. 'Birthright' hides a sound. Bekhorah ('firstborn right') and berakhah ('blessing') are built on the same three consonants, b-k-r and b-r-k, with the last two swapped. That is the wordplay Esau himself uses in Gen 27:36: 'he took my bekhorah, and see, now he has taken my birkhati.' The KJV's 'birthright' and 'blessing' are unrelated English words and lose the link. In this world the bekhorah meant a double share of the father's estate (Ibn Ezra, Radak) and the honour of leading the family, including the priestly role Rashi describes. What Jacob asks for is the family's future, and he is asking for it at a table.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'as the day'. Rashi reads it as 'clearly' (a sale as plain as the day), Radak as the kaf of truth, 'a complete sale today', Ramban as 'at this time'. The five English versions split between 'this day' and 'first'.
'Your birthright', from the same consonants as berakhah 'blessing' (b-r-k) with the last two letters swapped. Gen 27:36 uses the pair directly.

verses.translation_literal: And Esau said, “Behold, I [am] going to die; and for what [is] this to me, a birthright?”
verses.translation_dramatic: “Look at me,” said Esau. “I am going to die anyway. What good is a birthright to me?”
verses.directors_commentary:
Esau's answer is a line that is easy to over-read. The Hebrew 'I am going to die' (holekh lamut) is a participle of motion: 'I am on my way to dying'. The tradition splits on whether it is hunger-talk or a hunter's truth. Sforno: he is dying of exhaustion; Rashbam, Ibn Ezra and Radak: his trade is dangerous, with bears, lions and wild beasts, and he may die before his father, so a right that matters only after the father's death is worth nothing to him. Ramban says the same. The KJV's 'at the point to die' is a fair paraphrase and the ASV's 'about to die' is better.

The second clause uses a very contemptuous word order: 'and for what, this, to me, a birthright': the thing he is giving away is named last, as an afterthought, after the demonstrative 'this'. The KJV supplies 'profit' and 'do'; the Hebrew has neither, only 'what is this to me?'. Rashi's midrash makes the birthright a dangerous priestly service that Esau wants no part of; the plain text gives only his own present-minded appetite and fear.

philological_notes.note: 'Going to die': hunger hyperbole (Sforno) or the daily risk of hunting (Rashbam, Ibn Ezra, Radak). The text allows both.
'Why this to me': the expression of futility; there is no 'profit' in the Hebrew, only the shrug of a man who cannot see any use for it.

verses.translation_literal: And Jacob said, “Swear to me as the day.” And he swore to him; and he sold his birthright to Jacob.
verses.translation_dramatic: “Swear it,” said Jacob. “Swear it to me now.” And Esau swore. And so he sold his birthright to Jacob.
verses.directors_commentary:
Jacob does not trust the shrug. He asks for an oath, the binding speech of the ancient world, sworn by God's name, the thing that makes a spoken promise into a legal act. Sforno: the birthright is an intangible thing that cannot be handed over like a sheep, so the oath supplies the missing weight. Radak: Jacob fears that once Esau has eaten he will regret it. The same word kayyom appears again, 'as the day', and is read as in v.31.

The KJV 'sware' is archaic but exact. The Hebrew has the sequence in three short verbs: said, swore, sold. Ramban asks whether the oath came before or sealed the sale, and the text does not settle it. The text also never states a price beyond the meal of v.34; Rashbam and Radak's father supply money, and Sforno says the price was agreed and 'the text did not trouble to spell it out'. The narrator gives only the transaction, not the haggling.

philological_notes.note: Niphal imperative: 'swear!', literally 'bind yourself by seven / by oath'. A legal act, not a figure of speech.

verses.translation_literal: And Jacob gave to Esau bread and a stew of lentils; and he ate, and he drank, and he arose, and he went; and Esau despised the birthright.
verses.translation_dramatic: Jacob gave Esau bread and a bowl of lentil stew. He ate. He drank. He got up. He walked away. And that was how Esau despised his birthright.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four verbs in a row, ate, drank, arose, went, with no adjective and no pause: this is the narrator's most damning technique. Esau does not argue, does not bargain, does not look back. Then the verdict, in the narrator's own voice: vayyivez, 'and he despised'. The KJV's 'thus Esau despised his birthright' turns the verdict into a consequence ('thus') and adds the phrase 'went his way', a flavour absent from the plain Hebrew 'went'. The Hebrew does not say 'so' or 'thus'; it adds the verdict as one more flat verb in the chain, and the reader is left to see that the verdict is the same act as the walking away. Rashi says the text is testifying to his wickedness; Radak that even after eating he did not regret it; Ramban that the contempt shows in the fact that he went back to hunting.

The lentils (adashim) are the poor man's staple of the ancient Near East, red when split and hulled, as Radak notes, which explains the colour of v.30. Bread and lentils is an ordinary peasant meal, not a feast; Sforno proposes that Jacob gave the pot itself, in the manner of a symbolic exchange of goods like the sandal of Ruth 4:7. Ibn Ezra and Ramban debate whether Isaac was poor; the text does not say.

philological_notes.note: 'And he despised': an imperfect with the waw-consecutive, the narrator's verdict. The root means to hold in contempt, to treat as nothing. Rashbam notes the form is short for vayyivezeh.
Lentils: a staple pulse of the region. Hulled red lentils cook to a reddish stew, which Radak notes as the source of the colour.

events.title: Abraham takes Keturah, who bears six sons
events.narrative_summary: Abraham takes another wife, Keturah, who bears him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah. The text lists grandsons through Jokshan and Midian.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text gives no date ('Abraham again took a wife'). It comes after Sarah's death (Abraham 137, Gen 23) and before his death at 175 (v.7), and the births take years. Placed at Abraham's age about 150 from anchor.abraham_birth, margin 13 years to span 137-163, duration 10 years for the births. Tier MACRO_ERA: no numbered year in the text.

events.title: Abraham gives all to Isaac and sends the concubines' sons east
events.narrative_summary: Abraham gives all he has to Isaac, gives gifts to the sons of his concubines, and sends them east, away from Isaac, while he is still alive.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'While he was still alive' (v.6) puts it before his death at 175. Anchored on the end of the Keturah event with offset 5 years and margin 4 years so it stays between about 156 and 175. No exact date in the text, so MACRO_ERA.

events.title: Abraham dies at 175 and is gathered to his people
events.narrative_summary: Abraham lives 175 years, dies in a good old age, old and satisfied, and is gathered to his people.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Age 175 (v.7) from anchor.abraham_birth: offset 175 years, REGNAL_YEAR, margin one year since an age covers a whole year. Isaac is then 75 (175-100).

events.title: Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham at Machpelah
events.narrative_summary: His sons Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham in the cave of Machpelah, in the field Abraham bought from the Hittites, near Mamre, beside Sarah.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No delay is stated, and the text does not give the place of death. Isaac dwelt at Beer-lahai-roi (24:62, 25:11), so he would travel to Machpelah: urim travel gives about 149 km by road, 2.5 days hurrying (5 km/h) or 5 days walking (4 km/h); Ishmael must also come from his own place. Starts at the end of the death event with margin 7 days to cover the journey, gathering and mourning; REGNAL_YEAR as the scene falls under Abraham's age at death.

events.title: God blesses Isaac, who dwells at Beer-lahai-roi
events.narrative_summary: After Abraham's death, God blesses his son Isaac, and Isaac settles near the well Beer-lahai-roi.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'After the death of Abraham' (v.11) gives only order. Anchored on the end of the burial, duration 1 year and margin 1 year for the vague span of the blessing and settling. Rashi (Sotah 14a) reads the blessing as the comfort of mourners, which would fit the days right after the burial.

events.title: Ishmael dies at 137 and his sons settle from Havilah to Shur
events.narrative_summary: Ishmael lives 137 years, dies and is gathered to his people. His descendants dwell from Havilah to Shur, east of Egypt on the way to Assyria.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Ishmael was born when Abraham was 86 (16:16), so 137 years later is 223 years from anchor.abraham_birth. Offset 223 years, REGNAL_YEAR, margin 1 year. Isaac is then 123 and Jacob 63. The notice is placed here by the toledot structure and is not narrated at that point in time.

events.title: Isaac, aged forty, takes Rebekah as wife
events.narrative_summary: Isaac is forty years old when he takes Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram and sister of Laban, as his wife.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Isaac was forty years old' (v.20): offset 40 years from anchor.isaac_birth, REGNAL_YEAR, margin one year. Duration 7 days as a wedding week, a convention of the period and not stated here. Rashi counts Rebekah's birth at the binding, when Isaac was 37, and three years of waiting.
events.ancient_year_marker: When Isaac was forty years old

events.title: Isaac prays for barren Rebekah and she conceives
events.narrative_summary: Isaac entreats the LORD on behalf of his wife because she is barren; the LORD grants it and Rebekah conceives.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text gives no date, but Isaac was 40 at marriage (v.20) and 60 at the birth (v.26), so the barrenness lasted twenty years (Rashbam, Radak on v.26). Starts 19 years after the wedding week and lasts 3 months, so it ends near Isaac's 59 years and 3 months, about nine months (c. 270 days) before the birth at 60: the full term of v.24 ('her days were fulfilled'; Pseudo-Jonathan counts 270 days) sets the conception, and the struggle (vv.22-23) falls inside the pregnancy. Margin 6 months. REGNAL_YEAR since the ages frame the scene. The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan counts 22 years, which the 40/60 ages do not support.

events.title: Rebekah consults the LORD about the struggling children
events.narrative_summary: The children struggle within Rebekah; she asks why she is like this and goes to inquire of the LORD, who tells her two nations are in her womb and the elder will serve the younger.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: During the pregnancy, after the conception; set about 3 months after it ends, margin 2 months, before the delivery at Isaac's age 60. Duration 1 day for the inquiry. No explicit time word. Pseudo-Jonathan places the inquiry in the school of Shem and Eber.

events.title: Rebekah bears twins, Esau and Jacob
events.narrative_summary: When her days are complete Rebekah bears twins: Esau comes out first, red and hairy; Jacob follows holding Esau's heel. Isaac is sixty.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Isaac was sixty years old' (v.26): offset 60 years from anchor.isaac_birth, REGNAL_YEAR, margin one year. This agrees with anchor.jacob_birth, which is derived from the same verse. Duration 12 hours is an estimate for the delivery.

events.title: The boys grow: Esau the hunter, Jacob the tent-dweller
events.narrative_summary: The boys grow up. Esau becomes a skilful hunter and a man of the field; Jacob is a quiet man living in tents. Isaac loves Esau for his game, Rebekah loves Jacob.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'The boys grew' gives no number. Placed from 10 years to 20 years after the birth, margin 8 years. MACRO_ERA because nothing numbered is said. Pseudo-Jonathan has Jacob study in the house of Eber; Onkelos has him serve the house of study.

events.title: Esau sells his birthright to Jacob for lentil stew
events.narrative_summary: Esau comes in from the field exhausted and asks Jacob for the red stew he has cooked. Jacob asks for the birthright in exchange, Esau swears and sells it, eats and leaves, despising the birthright.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A single continuous scene on one day, at an unspecified time of the boys' adulthood; the text names no hour. Starts at the end of the growing-up span, margin 8 years, MACRO_ERA. Duration 2 hours for the meal and bargain. 'This day' (vv.31, 33) marks the same day. Pseudo-Jonathan says it was the day Abraham died, which would put this scene about 15 years after the birth of the twins (Jacob 15 at Abraham's death); this fragment does not adopt it.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Abraham's death leads his sons to bury him at Machpelah (25:8-9).
With Abraham dead, God turns the blessing to Isaac, who stays at Beer-lahai-roi (25:11).
The conception granted in answer to Isaac's prayer (25:21) leads, at the full term, to the birth of the twins (25:24).
Rebekah's conception after Isaac's prayer leads to the children struggling in her womb (25:21-22).

systems.name: Binding oath
systems.ancient_near_east_context: An oath fixed an agreement, calling on the deity as witness and making it hard to undo.
rules_and_mechanics: One party asks the other to swear.
The oath is sworn aloud before the transaction is carried out.
A sworn agreement cannot be undone.

systems.name: Transfer of the birthright
systems.ancient_near_east_context: The firstborn normally received a larger share of the inheritance and headship of the family. The text describes a transfer by sale to a younger brother, which Nuzi texts are sometimes cited to compare; the comparison is debated.
rules_and_mechanics: The birthright belongs to the firstborn by birth.
It can be given up in exchange for something of value.
The transfer is confirmed by an oath.

systems.name: Burial in the family tomb
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Burial with one's ancestors in a family tomb, often a cave, was central to Israelite and neighbouring cultures; a family grave on owned land also served as a claim to the land.
rules_and_mechanics: The heirs, usually the sons, bury the dead.
The dead is placed in the family's own tomb, beside earlier burials.
The tomb stands on land legally acquired by the family.

systems.name: Inheritance of the estate
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In the ancient Near East a patriarch could settle his property before death, giving one heir the bulk of it and lesser children gifts, then sending them off so they did not compete for the estate.
rules_and_mechanics: The patriarch can name a single heir for the whole estate while still alive.
Sons of secondary wives receive gifts rather than a share of the inheritance.
Those excluded are sent away from the heir, often to another region.

systems.name: Inquiry of the LORD
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Asking the deity about a puzzling event was common in the ancient Near East; it was done at a sanctuary or through a prophet or priest, and the answer came as a spoken oracle.
rules_and_mechanics: A person goes to inquire of the LORD about a troubling matter.
The LORD answers in direct speech.
The oracle announces the future of the persons concerned, not only the present.

systems.name: Petition prayer
systems.ancient_near_east_context: People appealed to the god for a need such as fertility, and the text reports the god as answering by changing the situation. Barrenness was a common reason for such appeals.
rules_and_mechanics: A person addresses the LORD with a specific request.
The LORD may grant it, and the narrative reports the result directly.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham in the cave of Machpelah, beside Sarah.
system_instances.significance_note: The brothers act together, and the burial confirms the first land owned in the promised land (Gen 23).

system_instances.outcome_summary: Esau gives up his birthright to Jacob for bread and lentil stew.
system_instances.significance_note: Shows Esau's disregard for his inheritance and Jacob's calculation, preparing for the blessing story of Gen 27.

system_instances.outcome_summary: At Jacob's demand Esau swears, and then sells the birthright.
system_instances.significance_note: The oath makes the sale binding in a way Esau cannot easily undo.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abraham gives all he has to Isaac and gifts to the other sons, then sends them east.
system_instances.significance_note: Settles the succession: the promise line goes through Isaac alone, and the other sons are kept apart from him.

system_instances.outcome_summary: After Abraham's death God blesses Isaac, who settles by Beer-lahai-roi.
system_instances.significance_note: God himself carries the blessing of Abraham on to Isaac.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac entreats the LORD for his barren wife; the LORD grants it and Rebekah conceives.
system_instances.significance_note: The line continues by prayer and God's answer, not by human power.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Rebekah asks the LORD why the children struggle; he says two nations are in her womb and the elder will serve the younger.
system_instances.significance_note: Announces the reversal of the usual order of birth, which frames the rest of the Jacob story.
